title: Web Crawler
summary: Crawl the web with a distributed, polite fleet of fetchers coordinated through a URL frontier.
narrative:
A web crawler is a deceptively simple loop wrapped around a brutal scaling problem. Start with a handful of seed URLs, fetch each page, pull the links out of it, and repeat — forever, across billions of pages, without duplicate work within a crawl generation or hammering any single site into the ground.

The heart of the design is the frontier: a message queue holding the URLs still to be visited. An operator seeds it through a coordinator, and a fleet of stateless worker fetchers pulls URLs off the queue, downloads each page, and pushes the newly discovered links back onto the frontier. Add more workers and you crawl faster; that is the whole point of decoupling the queue from the fetchers. Model front queues by priority and back queues per host; a host becomes eligible only after its next allowed fetch time. The Client here is the crawl operator, and the Web Server is the coordinator. A Task Scheduler registers periodic re-crawls and feeds due URLs into the frontier.

Normalize URLs before deduplication: strip fragments, normalize hosts and default ports, and apply an explicit policy for query parameters. A Bloom filter cheaply identifies definitely unseen URLs; confirm positive matches against exact visited state to avoid silently dropping unseen pages. Keep exact crawl metadata — each URL's last-crawled generation and content hash — in a key-value metadata table, and store the raw pages in Blob Storage; a matching content hash stops a duplicate page from being indexed twice. Claim each URL/generation with a conditional write to that metadata table before fetching, and expire failed claims for retry. Workers share a Cache for robots.txt and per-domain next-fetch timestamps; atomically reserve host slots before fetching and honor robots policies. Keep processed content in the Search Index, and optionally connect Workers to DNS with cached resolutions. Scheduled re-crawls create a new eligible generation instead of being blocked forever by the seen filter.

constraints: Seed URLs enter the frontier only through the coordinator
Only workers fetch pages and write to storage
capacity: Tens of billions of unique URLs tracked
specs.tradeoff: Bloom-filter membership uses space proportional to the number of URLs at a chosen false-positive rate; exact visited-state checks on positive matches prevent skipped pages. Priority front queues improve freshness while per-host back queues and shared timestamps enforce politeness. Periodic re-crawls trade bandwidth for freshness.
specs.bonus: Add Monitoring & Alerting to track fetch rate, frontier queue depth, and per-host politeness. Connect Workers to DNS for hostname resolution with cached results.

topologyRules.message: Operators steer the crawl through the Coordinator, never the fetcher fleet directly.
Seed URLs must enter the frontier through the Coordinator, not be injected straight into the queue.
A page only reaches storage after a Worker has fetched it from the frontier.

resilienceRules.message: Run a fleet of at least two fetchers; a crawler with one worker barely crawls.
Every fetcher must consult the Bloom Filter, or the crawl loops on URLs it has already seen.

hints: Model the crawl as a loop: the Client seeds the Coordinator (Web Server), which fills the Message Queue frontier; Workers pull URLs, fetch pages, and push new links back onto the queue.

Connect Workers to the Bloom Filter for URL screening, Blob Storage for raw pages, and the Cache for robots.txt and atomic host-delay reservations. Confirm Bloom positives against an exact key-value visited/content-hash table, and use generation-aware dedup so re-crawls remain possible.

Run two Workers, each wired to the frontier, Bloom Filter, Blob Storage, Search Index, Cache and DNS. Add Web Server → Task Scheduler → Message Queue for re-crawls and Web Server → Monitoring. Front queues prioritize URLs; per-host back queues enforce delays.
